title: Benchmarks
one_line_goal: Fair, repeatable tests vs Chrome, Edge and plain Tauri; first data collected
summary: Build a test bench that compares Ferrum with Chrome, Edge and a bare Tauri app under identical conditions. Check it against itself to learn the noise level, write predictions down in advance, then run the first test campaign. Data is only collected here; it is interpreted in P8.

tasks.title: Bare Tauri app to compare against
tasks.what: A minimal Tauri app with one web view, default settings and no Ferrum features, built on the same Tauri and WebView2 versions as Ferrum.
tasks.why: Without this baseline, any gain or loss could be Tauri's or WebView2's and not Ferrum's, and the paper could credit Ferrum with something it did not do.
tasks.how: Build it in release mode, load a test page with a small script, and save a comparison of its library versions against Ferrum's.
tasks.chain: We must show what Ferrum adds over plain Tauri → build a minimal app on the same Tauri and WebView2 versions with no Ferrum features → differences can be credited to Ferrum's design.
tasks.check: It builds and loads a test page; a version comparison with Ferrum shows only intended differences.

tasks.title: Ten local test workloads
tasks.what: Ten test workloads served from this PC: simple page, heavy web app, huge page, scrolling, many navigations, video, graphics, several active tabs, many background tabs, close and restore.
tasks.why: If a live site changes between two runs, the products are no longer tested on the same thing, and a difference in results could just be a different page.
tasks.how: Build each workload as fixed pages and settings served by the local test server, with one wiki page per workload that describes it.
tasks.chain: Results must not depend on live websites → build ten local workloads (simple page, heavy web app, huge page, scrolling, many navigations, video, graphics, several active tabs, many background tabs, close and restore) → every product sees exactly the same content.
tasks.check: Each workload has its page and an equivalence check; content is identical across two server starts.

tasks.title: A few real websites as extras
tasks.what: A short list of real public websites without login or Google sign-in, used as extra workloads.
tasks.why: Results only on our own test pages could miss how real sites behave. Mixing real sites into the main results would make them impossible to repeat.
tasks.how: Choose a few public sites that need no login and no Google sign-in, list them on the workload pages, and label them 'extra' everywhere they appear.
tasks.chain: Local pages may not reflect real use → pick a short list of public sites without login, with the visit date recorded → a reality check, clearly labelled extra, never the main result.
tasks.check: A dry run records the response and page size for each site; no results drawn from it.

tasks.title: Fair settings for each product
tasks.what: One versioned settings file per product, recording window size, cache, network, extensions, background throttling and the resource savers of Chrome and Edge.
tasks.why: Unrecorded settings let a comparison be tilted without anyone noticing. Switching off Chrome's or Edge's savers would make Ferrum look better than it is.
tasks.how: Keep one versioned file per product in the benchmarks folder for every relevant setting, with 'as shipped' and 'matched' versions if you choose both.
tasks.chain: Chrome and Edge have built-in resource savers → record every relevant setting per product in versioned files, never switching their savers off just to help Ferrum → the comparison is fair and anyone can check it.
tasks.check: Every settings file passes a format check; a diff report shows only the documented differences.

tasks.title: Test runner
tasks.what: A Rust program that plans and runs every trial: shuffled order with a recorded seed, a fresh profile each time, all processes tracked, and every trial recorded, failures included.
tasks.why: Running products in a fixed order or reusing old profiles can favour one of them. Dropping failed trials would hide problems and bias the averages.
tasks.how: Start each product paused inside a Windows process group (a Job Object) so its child processes are counted, save each trial before the next, and test with a dummy program.
tasks.chain: Trial order and leftovers can bias results → a Rust runner shuffles trials with a recorded seed, starts each product fresh with a clean profile, tracks all its processes, and records every trial including failures → runs are fair, resumable and complete.
tasks.check: The same seed gives the same plan; a test confirms child processes are tracked and failures recorded.

tasks.title: Scripts that drive each workload
tasks.what: One browser-automation script (Playwright, written in TypeScript) per workload, started by the test runner, writing one result file per trial.
tasks.why: If each product were driven by a different script, timing differences could come from the scripts and not from the products.
tasks.how: Connect to every product through the same debugging channel (Chrome DevTools Protocol), and run each script once on each product in a dry run.
tasks.chain: Each product must be driven the same way → one browser-automation script (Playwright) per workload, connecting to every product through the same debugging channel → differences come from the products, not the driver.
tasks.check: Each script runs once on each product, or the unsupported feature is named and recorded.

tasks.title: Record the setup and pin versions
tasks.what: A record of the setup for every run (Windows build, product versions, WebView2 runtime, power plan, display, background apps) and pinned browser versions.
tasks.why: If Chrome or Edge updated itself halfway through, the later trials would test a different browser, and the comparison would quietly break.
tasks.how: Download a fixed Chrome test build with a checksum, optionally a fixed WebView2 version, and block Edge updates; whether Edge updates can be blocked reliably is not yet confirmed.
tasks.chain: A silent browser update mid-campaign would spoil the data → record Windows build, product versions, power plan and background apps for each run, and pin browser versions → any change is caught and flagged.
tasks.check: A dry-run record has every field; a test flags a version change between two trials.

tasks.title: Smoothness measurement
tasks.what: Measurement of smoothness: how evenly frames are drawn while scrolling and animating, for each product.
tasks.why: An app can use little memory and still feel jerky. Without a smoothness measure, that downside would be invisible in the results.
tasks.how: Run the Windows tool PresentMon as a separate admin-level process aimed at the product, and collect long-frame data inside the page; whether PresentMon can tell products apart is not yet confirmed.
tasks.chain: Smooth scrolling and animation matter to users → measure frame timing with a Windows tool (PresentMon) and long-frame data inside the page → smoothness can be compared, or marked unsupported for a product.
tasks.check: A scrolling dry run gives frame data for each product, or the product is marked unsupported.

tasks.title: Energy, only if it can be measured honestly
tasks.what: Energy measurement, only if it can be done honestly: CPU energy counters, a wall-power meter if you have one, or else energy marked unsupported.
tasks.why: Energy numbers are easy to overstate. A wrong number in the paper would mislead readers more than an honest 'not measured'.
tasks.how: If you approve, a separate admin-level reader collects the processor's energy counters over each trial, labelled modelled CPU energy; whether this PC's processor exposes them is not yet confirmed.
tasks.chain: Energy use is worth reporting but hard to measure → if you approve, a separate admin-level reader collects CPU energy counters (labelled modelled, CPU only), or a wall-power meter is used → otherwise energy is marked unsupported, never estimated.
tasks.check: A dry run gives energy samples with units, or the energy measurements show unsupported with the reason.

tasks.title: Statistics pipeline
tasks.what: A Python pipeline that reads the run records and raw files and computes averages, spread, confidence ranges, effect sizes and corrections for many comparisons, plus plots.
tasks.why: Averages alone can make chance differences look real. Without proper statistics, the paper could claim a win that is only noise.
tasks.how: Write the pipeline in Python with pinned library versions; it reads the run records, computes the statistics and draws the plots, with tests on made-up data.
tasks.chain: Numbers need honest statistics → a Python pipeline computes averages, spread, confidence ranges, effect sizes and corrections for many comparisons, plus plots → the analysis is repeatable to the byte.
tasks.check: Tests on made-up data with known answers pass; two runs give identical output.

tasks.title: Measure the noise level
tasks.what: A check of the test bench itself: one setup compared against itself (an A/A test) plus short pilot runs for each experiment.
tasks.why: Without knowing the noise, a small difference could be taken as real, or too few trials could be run to see a real one.
tasks.how: Run the same product and settings as both sides of a comparison, then run short pilots of each experiment and use their spread to choose the trial counts.
tasks.chain: Some variation is just noise → run one product against itself (an A/A test) plus short pilots → we know the smallest real difference we can detect and set the trial count for each experiment.
tasks.check: A/A data saved; noise level reported; each experiment page states its trial count and why.

tasks.title: Write predictions before testing
tasks.what: Each prediction for the first campaign written down in advance, with the size of difference that would really matter and the analysis plan.
tasks.why: Choosing what counts as a win after seeing the data lets wishful thinking shape the result. Readers and reviewers can check that the plan came first.
tasks.how: For each prediction, write the difference that would really matter and the planned analysis on its page, then ask you to approve them.
tasks.chain: Deciding what counts as success after seeing data is biased → write each prediction and its meaningful-difference threshold first, and you approve them → results cannot be bent to fit.
tasks.check: Every prediction is recorded and approved by you before the first campaign starts.

tasks.title: First test campaign
tasks.what: The first test campaign: footprint, startup, page-load, smoothness, reliability, security-cost and isolation-cost experiments (and energy if supported) on Chrome, Edge, bare Tauri and Ferrum without sleeping.
tasks.why: Without a full first campaign there is no data for the paper, and no 'without sleeping' reference that P7's tab sleeping can be compared with.
tasks.how: Run every planned trial with the test runner, keeping failures, and save each experiment's run record, trials and checksums; nothing is interpreted yet.
tasks.chain: The bench is ready and checked → run the footprint, startup, page-load, smoothness, reliability, security-cost and isolation-cost experiments (and energy if supported) on Chrome, Edge, bare Tauri and Ferrum without sleeping → raw data for P8 and a reference for P7.
tasks.check: Each experiment has a complete raw-data folder with every trial and checksums; no results stated yet.

tasks.title: Reproduction guides
tasks.what: Two how-to guides: how we benchmark, and how to reproduce a campaign from a clean PC.
tasks.why: Results that only we can produce cannot be checked by anyone else, and reviewers may not accept them.
tasks.how: Write both guides step by step from a clean computer, using the exact commands, settings files and versions recorded during the campaigns.
tasks.chain: Others must be able to repeat our tests → write how-to guides for benchmarking and for reproducing a campaign on a clean PC → the research can be checked independently.
tasks.check: Following the guide on a fresh copy for one workload gives a valid run record.

tasks.title: Reading: benchmarking and statistics
tasks.what: A sixth batch of reading on benchmark methods and statistics for performance tests.
tasks.why: Methods invented without the field's guidance can contain known mistakes that reviewers spot at once, weakening every result.
tasks.how: Read the literature on benchmark methods and statistics for performance tests, and write one dated note per source.
tasks.chain: Methods must follow good practice → read the literature on benchmark methods and performance statistics → the method pages cite it.
tasks.check: New research notes saved; method pages cite them.

tasks.title: Gate and your review
tasks.what: The end-of-phase check and your review of the first campaign.
tasks.why: Lifecycle work in P7 is measured against this campaign. If the bench or its data had a flaw, every later comparison would inherit it.
tasks.how: Claude runs the gate script, which runs every check and saves the evidence; you then read the evidence and the campaign summary.
tasks.chain: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review the first campaign and approve; only then does P7 start.
tasks.check: All evidence files exist, the wiki check is clean, and you approve the end of P6.

test_gate.explanation: Code and tests pass → settings are proven fair → test pages and analysis give the same output every time → noise level known → you approve the predictions and check the PC → first campaign data is complete → you approve. Only then does P7 start.

rows.proves: Code is tidy and warning-free, all automatic tests pass, and the release build works.
Third-party libraries have acceptable licences and no known security problems.
Products differ only in the documented ways.
Test pages and the analysis give identical results on every run.
Noise level measured; trial counts justified.
Every planned trial recorded, failures included, none dropped.
Security, tabs and browsing tests still pass.
The plan pages are consistent and have no broken links.
You confirm no Chrome or Edge saver was switched off to help Ferrum.
You approved the predictions before any comparison ran.
Power plan, display and background apps are set as the guide says.
